summary: This best current practice sets out procedures for handling harassment at IETF meetings, virtual meetings, social events and on mailing lists. It defines how complaints are managed and enforced, and updates RFC 2418 with new working group guidelines and procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: This Best Current Practice sets procedures for reports of harassment during IETF activities. It defines who handles a report, when an investigation can begin, what remedies may be used, and how a decision can be appealed.

questions: how does the ietf handle harassment
how do i report harassment at an ietf meeting
what remedies can the ietf impose for harassment
how does the ietf harassment appeal work
subtitle: The IETF process for receiving, assessing, and acting on harassment reports.

tldr.problem: Some harassment in IETF activities is personal and may not disrupt a working group directly, so ordinary procedures for disruptive behavior may not address it well.
tldr.mechanism: An Ombudsteam receives confidential reports, offers advice, and may investigate with agreement from the Reporter and Subject. It can choose remedies and a defined appeal process reviews whether it exercised due diligence.
tldr.outcome: The RFC establishes procedures for handling reports and updates RFC 2418 and RFC 7437. The unit metadata says RFC 7776 is updated by RFC 8716.

today: RFC 7776 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 2418 and RFC 7437. The unit metadata says it is updated by RFC 8716.

sections.title: Why a Separate Procedure Exists
sections.content:
The IETF already has procedures for disruptive behavior in meetings and on mailing lists. This RFC addresses personal harassment that may not directly disrupt working-group progress but is still unacceptable between participants.

The procedures apply when other IETF policies do not apply or have been ineffective. They do not interfere with legal due process or release participants from contractual or corporate policies.
sections.plainLanguage: Some harassment needs a process beyond the rules for keeping meetings and mailing lists orderly. This RFC sets out that process for IETF activities.

sections.title: People and Terms in a Report
sections.content:
A Reporter brings a potential harassment concern to an Ombudsperson. A Respondent is the participant alleged to have engaged in the behavior, and the Subject is the person or group the behavior targeted. The Ombudsteam evaluates reports and may impose actions or remedies.

The RFC adopts a general definition of harassment as unwelcome hostile or intimidating behavior, including sexually aggressive behavior or intimidation based on personal attributes. It does not attempt to list every possible form or target attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the people involved so the process is clear: a Reporter raises a concern, a Respondent is accused of the behavior, and a Subject is affected by it. The Ombudsteam handles the report.

sections.title: The Ombudsteam
sections.content:
The IETF Chair appoints the Ombudsteam, which must comprise at least three people. Ombudspersons serve two-year terms, extended when needed to finish a report they lead. The Chair may reappoint or remove members under the procedures in the RFC.

Ombudspersons receive no compensation from the IETF. The IETF may fund training and professional advice, including legal and Human Resources advice.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF Chair appoints a team of at least three Ombudspersons. They serve two-year terms without compensation, and the IETF can fund training and professional advice.

sections.title: Receiving and Investigating a Report
sections.content:
Any IETF participant may report a concern to a serving Ombudsperson or to ombuds@ietf.org. The Ombudsteam can also provide confidential advice to participants who are unsure how to handle behavior. It MUST NOT begin a formal investigation without agreement from the Reporter and Subject.

A Lead Ombudsperson becomes the primary contact. The lead may offer advice or direct the matter to ordinary IETF procedures. Before imposing a remedy after an investigation, the Ombudsteam must contact the Respondent. The Respondent is not required to cooperate, but the team may consider a refusal when choosing a remedy.
sections.plainLanguage: A participant can report a concern to any Ombudsperson. The team can give advice, but a formal investigation requires agreement from the Reporter and Subject.

sections.title: Remedies and Their Purpose
sections.content:
If the Ombudsteam finds that harassment occurred, it chooses an appropriate response. Options can include a plan with the Respondent to prevent recurrence, mediation if both parties agree, referral to ordinary IETF procedures, or removal from a particular IETF activity.

The team remains responsible for the remedy and is expected to consider proportionality and reasonableness. Remedies aim to prevent escalation and repetition, not to punish. For a removal remedy, the Secretariat receives written notice of the remedy but not details about the harassment.
sections.plainLanguage: The Ombudsteam can choose a response suited to the report, from an agreed plan to removal from an activity. The aim is to stop escalation and prevent a repeat, not to punish.

sections.title: Appeals, Conflicts, and Confidentiality
sections.content:
A dissatisfied Subject, Reporter, or Respondent first discusses the decision with the Lead Ombudsperson and then the IETF Chair. A formal appeal is limited to whether the Ombudsteam exercised due diligence; it is not a new investigation or a negotiation over the remedy. For an immediate impact tied to an ongoing meeting, the Appeals Group must act within 24 hours.

People with a conflict of interest must recuse themselves completely from the process. The Ombudsteam is expected to protect confidentiality, keep secure records, and limit disclosure to what is needed for the process.
sections.plainLanguage: An appeal checks whether the Ombudsteam followed due process; it does not reopen the investigation or renegotiate the remedy. Anyone with a conflict must step away, and the process is confidential.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of this RFC contains no protocol security requirements. The document's procedures instead require secure handling of confidential records and information collected during reports and investigations.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not define a network security mechanism. Its process requires confidential case information and records to be handled securely.
